title: Floating and Sinking
summary: Why some objects float and others sink, how density and the upward push of water decide the result, and how ships, submarines, salty seas, and ice show this science at work.
poll: Heavy things always sink in water.

versions.title: Float or Sink?
versions.text:
Drop a rock in a tub. It will sink. Drop a cork in. It will float. Why?

Some things are heavy for their size. A rock is like that. It sinks. Some things are light for their size. Cork is like that. It floats.

Water can push up. It pushes on a boat. It pushes on you. The push holds up things that float.

A big ship is made of steel. Steel is heavy. So how can a ship float? The ship is hollow. It is full of air. Air is light. So the ship floats.

Salty water pushes up more. In the Dead Sea, the water is very salty. You can lie on top of it!

A submarine can sink. It can float, too. It has tanks. It fills the tanks with water. Then it sinks. It blows the water out. Then it floats up.

Ice floats, too. That is why ice sits on top of a cold drink.

versions.title: Float or Sink?
versions.text:
Drop a rock into a tub of water. It sinks fast. Drop in a cork. It bobs on top. Why do some things float and some things sink?

It is not just about how heavy a thing is. It is about how heavy it is for its size. A small rock is heavy for its size, so it sinks. A big log is light for its size, so it floats.

Water pushes up on things. When you swim, you can feel the push. It helps hold up things that float.

A big ship is made of steel, and steel is heavy. So how does a ship float? The ship is hollow. It is full of air, and air is light. So the whole ship is light for its size.

Salty water pushes up more than plain water. The Dead Sea is very salty. People can lie on top of it and read!

A submarine can sink and float. It has big tanks. When it fills the tanks with water, it sinks. When it blows the water out, it floats up.

Ice floats, too. That is why ice cubes sit at the top of a cold drink.

versions.title: Why Things Float or Sink
versions.text:
Drop a rock into a bucket of water, and it sinks to the bottom. Drop in a cork, and it bobs on top. Why do some things float while others sink?

The answer is not only about how heavy something is. It is about how heavy it is for its size. A small rock is heavy for its size, so it sinks. A huge log is light for its size, so it floats.

Water pushes up on everything that is in it. You can feel this push when you swim. The push helps hold up the things that float.

Ships are made of steel, and steel is very heavy. So how can a giant ship float? The ship is hollow inside. It is full of air, which is very light. That makes the whole ship light for its size.

Salty water pushes up harder than fresh water. The Dead Sea is so salty that people can lie on top of it and read a book!

A submarine can sink and float when it wants to. It has big tanks. To sink, it fills the tanks with water. To rise, it pushes the water out with air.

Ice floats, too. That is why ice cubes sit at the top of a glass of juice, and why ponds freeze on top first.

versions.title: Why Things Float or Sink
versions.text:
Drop a stone into a bucket of water, and it sinks straight to the bottom. Drop in a cork, and it bobs on the surface. Why do some objects float while others sink?

The answer is not only about weight. It is about how heavy something is for its size. A small stone is heavy for its size, so it sinks, but a huge log is light for its size, so it floats, even though it weighs much more than the stone.

Water pushes up on every object placed in it. You can feel this upward push when you swim. If the push is strong enough to hold up the object, the object floats.

Ships are made of steel, which is very heavy. So how can a giant ship float? The answer is its shape, because a ship is hollow and full of air, which is very light. Because of this, the whole ship is light for its size.

Salty water pushes up harder than fresh water. The Dead Sea is so salty that people can lie on the surface and read a book. An egg that sinks in a cup of tap water will float in very salty water.

A submarine can sink or rise whenever it needs to. It has large tanks, and to sink, it lets seawater fill the tanks. To rise, it blows air into the tanks and pushes the water out.

Ice floats, too. That is why ice cubes stay at the top of a drink, and why ponds freeze from the top down.

versions.title: The Science of Floating
versions.text:
Drop a stone into a bucket of water, and it drops straight to the bottom. Drop in a cork, and it bobs on the surface. Scientists explain this difference with an idea called density, which means how much matter is packed into a certain space.

Weight alone does not decide what floats. A pebble sinks, but a huge log floats even though it is much heavier, because the log is less dense than water and the pebble is denser.

Water also pushes upward on every object in it. This upward push is called buoyancy, and you can feel it when you swim. When an object enters water, it pushes some water out of the way, or displaces it. The more water an object displaces, the stronger the push.

Steel is much denser than water, so how can a steel ship float? A ship is hollow and filled with air. Its wide shape displaces a huge amount of water, so the buoyancy is strong enough to hold it up.

Salty water is denser than fresh water, so it pushes up harder. The Dead Sea is so salty that swimmers can lie on the surface and read. An egg that sinks in tap water will float in very salty water.

A submarine controls its depth with ballast tanks. To dive, it lets seawater flood the tanks. To rise, it blows air into them and forces the water out.

Ice floats, too. When water freezes, it expands, so ice is less dense than liquid water. That is why ponds freeze from the top down.

versions.title: Density, Buoyancy, and Archimedes
versions.text:
If you drop a stone into a bucket of water, it plunges directly to the bottom, but if you drop in a cork, it bobs contentedly on the surface. Scientists explain this contrast with a property called density, which describes how much mass is packed into a particular volume of a material.

Weight alone does not determine whether an object floats, because a tiny pebble sinks while an enormous log, which is considerably heavier, floats easily. The log is less dense than water, whereas the pebble is denser, and that comparison is what really matters.

More than two thousand years ago, the Greek mathematician Archimedes described the upward force that a liquid exerts on anything placed in it. According to his principle, an object in a liquid is pushed upward by a force equal to the weight of the liquid that it pushes aside. Scientists call this pushing aside displacement, and they call the upward force buoyancy. If the buoyancy becomes equal to the object's weight before the object is completely underwater, the object floats.

Steel is about eight times denser than water, so it seems surprising that a steel ship can stay afloat. The explanation lies in its shape, since a ship's hull is hollow and filled with air, which lowers its average density. Its broad hull also produces the displacement of an enormous amount of water, which creates enough buoyancy to support the ship.

Salty water is denser than fresh water, so it provides a stronger upward push. The Dead Sea is so salty that swimmers can lie back on the surface, and an egg that sinks in tap water will float in a strong salt solution.

Many fish and every submarine can change how they float. A bony fish adjusts the gas in a swim bladder inside its body, while a submarine uses ballast tanks, flooding them with seawater to dive and filling them with compressed air to rise again.

Ice floats because water expands as it freezes, so its molecules end up farther apart than they are in liquid water. As a result, lakes freeze from the top downward, and fish survive in the liquid water beneath the ice.

versions.title: Density, Buoyancy, and Archimedes
versions.text:
If a stone is dropped into a bucket of water, it plunges directly to the bottom, whereas a cork, dropped under identical circumstances, bobs contentedly on the surface. Scientists account for this contrast by invoking a fundamental physical property called density, which describes precisely how much mass is concentrated within a particular volume of a given material.

Weight alone does not determine whether an object floats, because a tiny pebble sinks immediately while an enormous log, considerably heavier in absolute terms, floats with apparent effortlessness. The log is less dense than water, whereas the pebble is significantly denser, and it is this comparative relationship, rather than raw weight, that genuinely determines the outcome.

More than two thousand years ago, the Greek mathematician Archimedes formulated a description of the upward force that any liquid exerts upon an object immersed within it. According to his principle, such an object experiences an upward force precisely equal to the weight of the liquid it displaces, and scientists refer to this displaced volume as displacement while describing the resulting upward force as buoyancy. Whenever that buoyancy becomes equal to the object's own weight before it is fully submerged, the object remains floating at the surface indefinitely.

Steel is approximately eight times denser than water, so it initially seems remarkable that an enormous steel ship can remain afloat at all. The explanation lies entirely in its engineering, since a ship's hull is hollow and predominantly occupied by air, which considerably reduces its average density, while its broad, deep hull simultaneously accomplishes the displacement of a truly tremendous quantity of water, generating sufficient buoyancy to support the entire vessel together with its cargo.

Salty water is appreciably denser than fresh water, so it provides a considerably stronger upward push. The Dead Sea, indeed, is so extraordinarily salty that swimmers can recline effortlessly upon its surface without any exertion whatsoever, and an egg that sinks promptly in ordinary tap water will float readily in a sufficiently concentrated salt solution.

Numerous fish species and every submarine ever constructed can regulate their own buoyancy quite deliberately. A bony fish adjusts the quantity of gas contained within a swim bladder situated inside its body, whereas a submarine instead relies on ballast tanks, flooding them with seawater in order to descend and subsequently filling them with compressed air in order to ascend once again.

Ice floats for a related reason: water expands as it solidifies, so its molecules become arranged within a crystalline pattern in which they are positioned considerably farther apart than they are within liquid water. Consequently, lakes freeze from the surface downward rather than from the bottom upward, and aquatic creatures survive comfortably in the liquid water that persists beneath the insulating layer of ice above them, a principle equally present in a bucket, a sea, and a submarine's tanks alike.

From Archimedes' ancient insight about displaced liquid to the modern hull of a steel cargo ship, the same single idea, that buoyancy must match weight before anything will float, explains every case considered here, whether the object is a drifting log, a swim bladder, or an entire frozen lake.

versions.title: Density, Buoyancy, and Archimedes
versions.text:
If a stone is dropped into a bucket of water, it plunges directly and immediately to the bottom, whereas a cork, dropped under identical circumstances, bobs contentedly and indefinitely upon the surface. Scientists account for this striking contrast by invoking a fundamental physical property called density, which describes precisely how much mass is concentrated within a particular volume of any given material.

Weight alone does not determine whether an object ultimately floats, because a tiny pebble sinks immediately while an enormous log, considerably heavier in absolute terms, floats with apparent effortlessness. The log is less dense than the surrounding water, whereas the pebble is significantly denser than it, and it is precisely this comparative relationship, rather than raw weight by itself, that genuinely determines the eventual outcome in every such case.

More than two thousand years ago, the Greek mathematician Archimedes formulated a rigorous description of the upward force that any liquid invariably exerts upon an object immersed within it. According to his famous principle, such an object experiences an upward force precisely equal to the weight of the liquid that it displaces, and scientists accordingly refer to this displaced volume as displacement, while describing the resulting upward force itself as buoyancy. Whenever that buoyancy becomes exactly equal to the object's own weight before it is entirely submerged, the object remains floating at the surface indefinitely rather than continuing to sink.

Steel is approximately eight times denser than ordinary water, so it initially seems genuinely remarkable that an enormous steel ship can remain afloat at all under such circumstances. The explanation, however, lies entirely in its careful engineering, since a ship's hull is hollow and predominantly occupied by air rather than solid metal, which considerably reduces its overall average density, while its broad, deep hull simultaneously accomplishes the displacement of a truly tremendous quantity of water, thereby generating sufficient buoyancy to support the entire vessel together with its cargo and crew.

Salty water is appreciably denser than fresh water, so it inevitably provides a considerably stronger upward push on anything placed within it. The Dead Sea, indeed, is so extraordinarily, almost absurdly salty that swimmers can recline effortlessly upon its surface without any exertion whatsoever, and an egg that sinks promptly in ordinary tap water will instead float quite readily in a sufficiently concentrated salt solution.

Numerous fish species and every submarine ever constructed can regulate their own buoyancy quite deliberately and with considerable precision. A bony fish adjusts the precise quantity of gas contained within a swim bladder situated deep inside its body, whereas a submarine instead relies on ballast tanks, flooding them with seawater in order to descend toward the depths and subsequently filling them with compressed air in order to ascend once again toward the surface.

Ice floats for a closely related reason: water expands measurably as it solidifies into a crystalline solid, so its molecules become arranged within a rigid, repeating pattern in which they are positioned considerably farther apart than they ever are within ordinary liquid water. Consequently, lakes and ponds freeze from the surface downward rather than from the bottom upward, and aquatic creatures survive comfortably within the liquid water that persists beneath the insulating layer of ice above them, a single unifying principle equally at work in a simple household bucket, an entire salty sea, and the carefully engineered ballast tanks of a submarine alike.

From Archimedes' ancient insight concerning displaced liquid all the way to the modern, carefully engineered hull of a steel cargo ship, the same single unifying idea, namely that buoyancy must come to equal weight before anything will truly float, explains every single case considered here, whether the object under discussion happens to be a drifting log, a fish's swim bladder, or an entire frozen lake.

MID.prompt: Explain how a heavy steel ship can float. Use the words density, buoyancy, and displace in your answer.
checklist: I explained that the ship is hollow and full of air.
I used density, buoyancy, and displace correctly.
I connected the ship's shape to the upward push of water.
MID.modelAnswer: A steel ship can float even though steel is much denser than water because of its shape. The ship is hollow and filled with air, so its wide hull pushes aside, or displaces, an enormous amount of water. The more water it displaces, the stronger the upward push of buoyancy becomes, and that buoyancy ends up strong enough to support the ship's heavy weight.

HIGH.prompt: Use Archimedes' principle to explain why the same ship floats higher in the Dead Sea than in a freshwater lake. Use displacement and density in your answer.
checklist: I stated Archimedes' principle in my own words.
I explained how water density changes the amount of displacement needed.
I used evidence from the article to support my answer.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Archimedes' principle says that an object floating in water is pushed upward by a force equal to the weight of the water it displaces. Because salty water like that in the Dead Sea has a higher density than fresh water, each unit of displacement provides a stronger upward push, since the same volume of salty water weighs more. This means the ship does not need to displace as much water to support its weight, so its hull sits higher in the Dead Sea than it would in a freshwater lake, the same way an egg floats in salty water but sinks in tap water.
